Question: Why does holding breath slow down heart rate? Heart function isn't under voluntary control, so how is it that the heart is able to slow down?
Answer: It is true that normally you don’t consciously control your heart rate since it falls within the ambit of autonomic control. However, you can intentionally affect this autonomic nervous system with some conscious hacks such as mind relaxation (meditation) techniques since these methods control your emotions or you can employ breathing mechanics to hack into vasopressor control which will affect the autonomic control of the heart. During inhalation, the thoracic cavity volume increases and its pressure falls. The aorta is decompressed and blood pressure falls. In a bid to raise and normalize blood pressure, the baroreflex kicks in and activates the sympathetic nervous system, and this increases the heart rate. The converse is true. When you exhale and hold your breath, the thoracic pressure increases, the aorta is compressed, and blood pressure rises. The baroreflex steps in a bid to to reduce and normalize blood pressure by activating the parasympathetic nervous system, and this reduces the heart rate. Another thing is that as the lungs recoil (relax) when you exhale and hold your breath, sensory receptors pick up the signals, and the parasympathetic nervous system is activated to reduce the heart rate. Also, carbon dioxide accumulation when you hold your breath can numb the brain, and this will activate the parasympathetic nervous system to decrease the heart rate.

Question: Is an increased resting heart rate a sign of needing more oxygen? If so, what are some ways to address this issue?
Answer: Yes. Good tissue oxygenation decreases the heart rate while lower blood levels of oxygen increase the heart rate. Stress will activate the sympathetic nervous system which leads to increased metabolism that raises oxygen demand. High performance athletes usually have low resting heart rates due to adaptations gleaned from regular exercise which increase oxygen saturation. These include a stronger heart, an improved breathing technique, the development of collateral blood vessels, increased number of red blood cells, and raised levels of hemoglobin, myoglobin, and mitochondria. Regular exercise will improve tissue oxygenation and lower the heart rate. Stress management will reduce sympathetic output and tissue oxygen demands which will reduce the heart rate.

Question: Can walking in cold weather trigger an asthma attack? If so, what is the reason behind it?
Answer: Yes. Cold weather causes skeletal muscle contraction, to generate heat, through increased sympathetic nervous system activation. The diaphragm is worked by the phrenic nerve which, in part, is sympathetic (also motor and sensory). This means that cold weather may cause the spasm of the diaphragm, a skeletal muscle, especially in asthmatic patients, and this can provoke asthmatic symptoms. This is especially true as cold weather also activates mast cells to degranulate, and secrete histamine that causes airway smooth contraction, which gives the symptoms of asthma.

Question: How can one prevent or alleviate dizziness while in bed? How long does dizziness typically last after waking up? Is it common to experience dizziness upon waking up?
Answer: As you sleep your blood pressure drops, given that the parasympathetic nervous system is activated, and muscles have become too weak to pump blood in the veins back to the heart for redistribution into systemic tissues and organs. As you stand, blood very well pools in the veins of the legs and this leads to postural hypotension (orthostatic hypotension). Perfusion of the brain and inner ear where perception and balance are effected is poor consequent to hypotension. The combination of these effects leads to dizziness . To remedy this, get out of bed slowly, and sit on the bed for a while to permit the sympathetic nervous system to switch on and muscles to regain their normal strength. You can look at dimmed light and/or exercise your leg muscles for a while as you sit on the bed, and this will activate the sympathetic nervous system and raise cortisol levels that will normalize your blood pressure.
